issues.claim: And which part of the application should not depend on the UI framework at all?
issues.problem: The second sentence of the hint nearly states step 5 of the reference answer, the UI-agnostic view model layer, so it gives away part of the answer.
issues.suggestedFix: Drop that sentence or soften it, for example: 'Which decision is easy to change later, and which one forces you to rewrite every view? What would you do to make a wrong choice cheaper?' Apply the same change to the ru hint.

issues.problem: The link is a source repository, not documentation. The MIT licence, the Skia default and the platform list are only partly visible in the fetched excerpt.
issues.suggestedFix: Use kind: article, or add a link to the Avalonia docs on rendering and platform support. The claims themselves are correct.

issues.claim: it ships and is serviced on the Windows App SDK lifecycle, separate from .NET
issues.problem: The cited WinUI 3 page says only that WinUI is delivered as part of the Windows App SDK. It does not show the separate lifecycle. The claim is true, but no cited source shows it.
issues.suggestedFix: Optionally add a link to the Windows App SDK support policy or release channels page and its title in linkTitles.

issues.claim: Which types do the binding engines of all three frameworks understand in the same way, and which types does each framework define for itself?
issues.problem: The hint points fairly directly at the contrast between options c and b/d. It is still a nudge, not the answer.
issues.suggestedFix: Make it a bit less direct, for example: 'What would break if the library had to compile without any reference to a UI framework?' Apply the same change to the ru hint.

issues.claim: all three frameworks install their own `SynchronizationContext`
